questions.question: A text editor must undo the most recent edit first. Which structure best stores the undo history?
options: A FIFO queue
A min-heap keyed by edit timestamp
A LIFO stack
An unsorted list scanned for the newest edit
questions.explanation: Undo needs last-in-first-out access, and a stack gives O(1) push and pop of the newest edit. A queue would hand back the oldest edit instead.

questions.question: Which java.util type does the Java documentation point to as the preferred LIFO stack implementation?
options: java.util.Stack, since it is the named stack class
PriorityQueue with a reverse comparator
Vector, because it is synchronized
ArrayDeque
questions.explanation: The Deque docs recommend ArrayDeque as a stack: it beats the legacy synchronized Stack and avoids LinkedList's per-node allocation and pointer chasing.

questions.question: A graph traversal must visit every node at distance 1 before any node at distance 2. Which structure drives that order?
options: A stack
A queue
A max-heap of node degrees
Recursion using the JVM call stack
questions.explanation: Breadth-first order needs FIFO: neighbours are enqueued as they are discovered and leave in discovery order, so all distance-1 nodes are processed first.

questions.question: Why do linked-list routines so often allocate a dummy (sentinel) node in front of the real head?
options: It stores the length, making size() O(1)
It makes the list circular and doubly linked
It removes the special case of inserting or deleting the head
It halves the number of pointer hops during traversal
questions.explanation: With a sentinel every real node has a predecessor, so head changes need no separate branch; the method simply returns dummy.next at the end.

questions.question: For a list of exactly 6 nodes, which node does slow point to once this loop ends?
options: The 3rd node, the first of the two middle nodes
The 4th node, the second of the two middle nodes
The 5th node
The last node
questions.explanation: fast moves twice as fast, so slow lands at index n/2; with n = 6 that is index 3, the second of the two middles. Stopping at the first middle needs a different guard.

questions.question: Appending to an ArrayList that doubles its backing array when full: which pair of costs is exact?
options: O(1) amortized and O(1) worst case
O(log n) amortized and O(n) worst case
O(1) amortized and O(n) worst case
O(n) amortized and O(n) worst case
questions.explanation: A growth step copies everything, costing O(n), but doubling makes copies rare: n appends total O(n) work, so O(1) amortized with an O(n) worst-case single append.

questions.question: Reversing a singly linked list of n nodes: how does auxiliary space compare between the recursive and iterative versions?
options: Recursion O(n) call stack, iteration O(1)
Both are O(1)
Recursion O(1), because Java optimises tail calls
Recursion O(log n), iteration O(n)
questions.explanation: Every recursive call holds a frame until the base case returns, so depth n costs O(n) stack. The loop keeps only prev, curr and next, and the JVM does no tail-call elimination.

questions.question: What is the tightest bound on this loop over a java.util.LinkedList holding n elements?
options: O(n), since each get is O(1)
O(n log n)
O(n) amortized, O(n log n) worst case
questions.explanation: LinkedList.get(i) walks from the nearer end, so index i costs O(i); summing that over all i is O(n^2). A for-each or Iterator would make the same scan O(n).

questions.question: Scanning n ints in order is usually far faster from an array than from a linked list. What is the main reason?
options: Array scanning has a lower asymptotic complexity
Contiguous memory lets one cache line serve many elements
Linked lists must be kept sorted to be traversed
Array access skips the JVM's bounds checking
questions.explanation: Both scans are O(n), but array elements share cache lines and are prefetched, while linked nodes sit scattered on the heap so each hop risks a cache miss.

questions.question: This deque code reports the maximum of every window of size k. What is its total running time over n elements?
options: O(n k)
O(n log k)
O(n log n)
O(n)
questions.explanation: Each index is added once and removed at most once, so the inner while loop performs O(n) pops in total across the entire scan, giving amortized O(1) per element.

questions.question: You rewrite a deep recursive DFS as a loop with an explicit ArrayDeque of frames. What is the real benefit?
options: The traversal order becomes breadth-first
Auxiliary space drops to O(1)
Frames move to the heap, so deep inputs avoid StackOverflowError
The time complexity improves by a logarithmic factor
questions.explanation: The same O(depth) state is still stored, but on the heap, bounded by available memory rather than the fixed JVM thread stack. Visit order and time cost are unchanged.

questions.question: Deciding whether a sorted int array contains two values summing to a target. Which approach is best in time and space?
options: Two pointers from both ends: O(n) time, O(1) extra space
HashSet of seen values: O(n) time, O(n) extra space
Binary search for each element: O(n log n) time
Nested loops over all pairs: O(n^2) time, O(1) space
questions.explanation: Sortedness lets you shrink the range deterministically: move left up when the sum is too small, right down when too large. One linear pass, no extra storage.

questions.question: Why can a DFS with an explicit stack report a longer hop count than BFS on an unweighted graph?
options: DFS cannot detect already-visited nodes
DFS can settle a node via a deep path before the short one
DFS always uses more memory, forcing early termination
DFS reaches only a spanning subset of the vertices
questions.explanation: LIFO order dives deep first, so a node may be finalised along a long path. BFS's FIFO order settles nodes in nondecreasing distance, which is what guarantees shortest hops.

questions.question: A queue built from an in-stack and an out-stack refills the out-stack only when it is empty. What does one dequeue cost?
options: O(n) amortized
O(log n) amortized
O(1) worst case
O(1) amortized, O(n) worst case
questions.explanation: Each element is moved between the two stacks at most once, so m operations cost O(m) overall, yet the single dequeue that triggers a transfer touches up to n elements.

questions.question: In Floyd's cycle detection the pointers meet inside the cycle, then one restarts at the head and both step by one. Where do they meet?
options: The node where the cycle begins
The node halfway around the cycle
The node just before the earlier meeting point
The same meeting point as before
questions.explanation: If the tail before the cycle has length m, the meeting point lies exactly m steps from the cycle entry, so m single steps from the head and from the meeting point converge there.

questions.question: Test whether a singly linked list is a palindrome in O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Which plan meets both limits?
options: Push every value on a stack, then re-walk and pop to compare
Copy the values into an array and use two pointers
Find the middle, reverse the second half in place, compare, restore
Recurse to the tail and compare while the calls unwind
questions.explanation: Only in-place reversal avoids extra storage. The stack and array copies both need O(n) space, and the recursive version keeps O(n) frames on the call stack.

questions.question: Array a holds positive ints. What is the tightest bound on this loop's running time?
options: O(n^2), because a while loop is nested in the for loop
O(n log n)
O(n) on average but O(n^2) in the worst case
O(n), since i only ever moves forward, at most n times
questions.explanation: The inner while never rewinds i, so it executes at most n times across the whole run. The nesting is amortized, not multiplicative, giving a linear total.

questions.question: A dynamic array doubles when full and halves when it drops below one quarter full. What does a push or pop cost?
options: O(log n) amortized
O(1) amortized, with occasional O(n) resizes
O(n) amortized, because resizes can cascade
O(1) worst case for every single operation
questions.explanation: The one-quarter shrink threshold leaves slack after each resize, so at least n/2 cheap operations must happen before the next one, spreading the O(n) copies to O(1) each.
